chunks: Sa'd ibn Abd Allah narrated from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), from al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Fadhl, from Abd Allah ibn Bukayr, from Zurarah, who said: I said to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him):

My mother had made a vow upon herself that if God restored to her some of her children from an ailment she feared for them, she would fast on that day on which the remainder of them arrived. So she traveled with us to Mecca, and it became unclear to us; we did not know whether she should fast or break her fast. He said: 'She should not fast, for God Almighty has lifted the obligation of her vow from her, and she fasts what she made upon herself.' I said: 'What do you think if she returns home, should she make up for it?' He said: 'No.' I said: 'So she leaves it?' He said: 'No, for I fear she will see in what she vowed that which she dislikes.'

key_terms.تَرَى فِيهِ مَا تَكْرَهُ: She sees in it that which she dislikes
key_terms.وَضَعَ اللَّهُ عَنْهَا حَقَّهُ: God lifted its obligation from her

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on fulfilling a vow to fast when the condition for the vow (such as the return of loved ones) is uncertain during travel?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (peace be upon him) distinguishes between the divine obligation of fasting and the voluntary vow (nadhr), ruling that the woman is exempt from fasting while traveling due to the uncertainty of her children's return, as God has lifted the burden during transit. She is instructed not to abandon the vow entirely but to fulfill it upon her return to the home, ensuring she does not incur regret by failing to complete the specific commitment she made to God.
